title: Episode 245: Daniel Webster: 'Liberty and Union, Now and Forever', the Dartmouth Case, and the Defender of the Constitution
description:
The thunderous life of Daniel Webster: the 'Godlike Daniel' whose dark eyes and resonant voice mesmerized the nation, defending Dartmouth College before the Supreme Court, crushing nullification with Robert Hayne, and sacrificing his reputation in the Seventh of March speech.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, our chronicle of the Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans follows the greatest orator in American history, whose thunderous eloquence defined the sacred indivisibility of the American Union: Daniel Webster.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: BLACK DAN OF NEW HAMPSHIRE AND DARTMOUTH COLLEGE
Born in 1782 in Salisbury, New Hampshire, on the rocky, snow-swept northern frontier, Daniel Webster was a sickly, dark-complexioned child whose piercing, coal-black eyes and craggy brow earned him the childhood nickname 'Black Dan'. His father Ebenezer Webster, a veteran of the French and Indian War and the Revolution, mortgaged his farm to send young Daniel to Dartmouth College. In Hanover, Webster blossomed into a brilliant debater, reading Cicero and Milton until he had memorized long passages of classical prose. Following graduation, he established a lucrative law practice in Portsmouth and Boston, rapidly earning a national reputation as the premier constitutional advocate in America. In 1818, Webster returned to Washington to defend his beloved alma mater before the Supreme Court in Dartmouth College v. Woodward. When the state of New Hampshire attempted to seize control of the private college, Webster delivered a four-hour oral argument that reduced Chief Justice John Marshall to tears: 'Sir, you may say that this is a small matter, and that is very true; it is, sir, as I have said, a small college. And yet there are those who love it!' Marshall ruled in Webster's favor, establishing the sanctity of private contracts and constitutional protections for private corporations across the United States.  At Dartmouth, young Webster was chosen to deliver the town's Fourth of July address at age eighteen, astonishing local farmers with his mature political philosophy and classical oratorical poise.  Webster's brother Ezekiel had sacrificed his own education to work the New Hampshire family farm so that Daniel could attend college, a fraternal sacrifice that Webster honored throughout his life.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: PLYMOUTH ROCK AND BUNKER HILL: THE VOICE OF THE REPUBLIC
In the 1820s, Webster became the undisputed voice of American civic religion, delivering monumental orations on the sacred anniversaries of national history. In December 1820, at the bicentennial of the landing of the Pilgrims at Plymouth Rock, five thousand listeners wept as Webster summoned the ghosts of the Mayflower pioneers, demanding that Americans preserve their religious and democratic heritage. In June 1825, at the laying of the cornerstone of the Bunker Hill Monument in Charlestown, before forty thousand spectators including forty surviving veterans of the battle and the Marquis de Lafayette, Webster spoke with the majestic authority of an Old Testament prophet. Wearing a tailored blue coat with polished brass buttons and a buff waistcoat—the colors of Washington's Continental Army—Webster possessed a commanding physical presence, a massive chest, and a deep, cathedral-like baritone voice that could carry across outdoor fields to twenty thousand people without amplification. Contemporaries referred to him simply as 'the Godlike Daniel'.  Webster's Bunker Hill oration was witnessed by an enormous throng that included revolutionary veterans weeping in the front rows, their trembling hands reaching out to touch the great orator's coat.  Webster's oration on the deaths of Thomas Jefferson and John Adams in August 1826 in Faneuil Hall included his famous invented speech for John Adams: 'Sink or swim, live or die, survive or perish, I give my hand and my heart to this vote!'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE WEBSTER-HAYNE DEBATE: JANUARY 1830
In January 1830, in the United States Senate, Webster delivered what is universally recognized as the greatest speech ever uttered on the floor of the American Congress. What began as a routine debate over western land sales escalated into an existential confrontation over the nature of the Constitution between Senator Robert Y. Hayne of South Carolina—speaking the nullification philosophy of John C. Calhoun—and Daniel Webster of Massachusetts. For two days, Hayne attacked New England, arguing that the Constitution was a compact between sovereign states and that any state possessed the sovereign right to nullify federal laws or secede from the Union. On the morning of January 26, 1830, the Senate galleries were jammed to the rafters with hundreds of spectators who had traveled through snowstorms from Philadelphia, Baltimore, and New York. When Webster rose from his desk, the chamber fell into pin-drop silence.  In the Senate chamber, listeners were captivated by Webster's dark, smoldering eyes, which contemporaries described as glowing coals beneath the cavernous arch of his monumental forehead.  During the Webster-Hayne debate, Vice President John C. Calhoun presided over the Senate, listening with visible agitation as Webster dismantled his beloved philosophy of nullification before the world.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: 'LIBERTY AND UNION, NOW AND FOREVER, ONE AND INSEPARABLE!'
In his historic 'Second Reply to Hayne', speaking for four continuous hours over two days with barely a note in his hand, Webster demolished the doctrine of nullification with devastating logic and soaring patriotic poetry. He refuted Hayne's claim that the Constitution was a fragile league of sovereign states, thundering that the federal government was 'the people's Constitution, the people's government, made for the people, made by the people, and answerable to the people.' He warned of the apocalyptic horrors that would follow if the doctrine of secession prevailed: a continent fractured into warring, petty states drenched in fraternal blood. In his immortal peroration, Webster prayed that his final earthly vision would not be of 'a land rent with civil feuds, or drenched, it may be, in fraternal blood', but of the glorious American Republic standing united under one banner: 'Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!' Webster's speech was reprinted in thousands of newspapers, memorized by millions of schoolchildren across the northern states, and forged the mystical nationalist consciousness that later inspired hundreds of thousands of Union soldiers to march into battle to save the United States.  Webster's concluding sentence in the Second Reply to Hayne became a sacred national motto, engraved in granite on public monuments, courthouses, and schools throughout the northern states.  Webster's Second Reply to Hayne was hailed by Supreme Court Justice Joseph Story as the greatest constitutional defense of the Union ever produced by an American statesman.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: SECRETARY OF STATE: THE WEBSTER-ASHBURTON TREATY OF 1842
In 1841, President William Henry Harrison appointed Webster as Secretary of State, an office he continued under John Tyler. Confronted with the dangerous 'Aroostook War'—a simmering border crisis between Maine and British Canada that threatened to draw the two nations into war—Webster engaged in brilliant personal diplomacy with British special envoy Lord Ashburton. Over glasses of fine port and dinners at Webster's home, the two statesmen resolved the dispute, signing the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842. The treaty peacefully settled the boundary dispute between Maine, New Brunswick, and the Great Lakes, established extradition procedures for criminals, and committed joint naval patrols off West Africa to suppress the transatlantic slave trade. When all other Whig cabinet members resigned in protest over Tyler's vetoes, Webster remained at his post until the treaty was ratified, putting international peace and national honor above partisan politics.  The Webster-Ashburton Treaty established the first permanent international commission to regulate shared waterways between the United States and Canada, creating a model for peaceful diplomatic arbitration.  The Webster-Ashburton Treaty established the 45th parallel as the northern border of Vermont and New York, resolving disputes that had lingered since the Treaty of Paris in 1783.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SEVENTH OF MARCH SPEECH: THE SACRIFICE OF REPUTATION: 1850
In the winter of 1850, as the nation teetered on the brink of civil war over slavery in the new territories, Webster performed the most controversial, sacrificial act of his political career. For decades, New England abolitionists had looked to Webster as their northern champion against the Slave Power. But on March 7, 1850, sixty-eight-year-old Webster rose in the Senate to support Henry Clay's omnibus compromise, delivering his celebrated 'Seventh of March Speech'. He began with words that silenced the chamber: 'I wish to speak to-day, not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man, but as an American, and a member of the Senate of the United States. I speak to-day for the preservation of the Union. Hear me for my cause.' In the speech, Webster endorsed the hated Fugitive Slave Law, arguing that the South had legitimate constitutional grievances and that preserving the Union took precedence over all other considerations. The reaction in Massachusetts was instantaneous and incandescent: northern abolitionists denounced Webster as a traitor; Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote: 'Every drop of blood in that man's veins has eyes that look downward'; and John Greenleaf Whittier published his scathing poem 'Ichabod', mourning Webster as an angel fallen into darkness. Yet Webster knew the price: he had knowingly sacrificed his personal reputation and his lifelong dream of the presidency to buy eleven years of peace for the Union.  Following the Seventh of March speech, abolitionists in Boston hung black mourning crepe outside their shop windows, yet southern moderates praised Webster for preserving national peace.  Following the Seventh of March speech, Webster received letters of praise from business leaders and moderates across the country who credited him with saving the nation from immediate civil war.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: MARSHFIELD BY THE SEA AND THE LEGEND OF DANIEL WEBSTER
Retiring to his beloved ocean estate of Green Harbor at Marshfield, Massachusetts, Webster spent his final months walking along the Atlantic beaches, gazing at his herd of white-faced oxen, and sailing his small fishing boat. On October 24, 1852, surrounded by his family and devoted farmhands, Daniel Webster passed away at the age of seventy, his final spoken words echoing across the room: 'I still live.' In American folklore, Stephen Vincent Benét immortalized him in the classic short story The Devil and Daniel Webster, depicting the legendary orator arguing for the soul of an American farmer before a jury of historical villains and beating the Devil himself through the sheer majesty of American freedom. Daniel Webster was a flawed giant, but his thundering eloquence gave voice to the indestructible spirit of the American constitutional nation, leaving behind a legacy summarized by his immortal words: Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable.  At Marshfield, Webster had lanterns hung in the rigging of his favorite fishing boat so he could gaze upon the fluttering American flag from his bedroom window as he lay dying.  Webster's personal charisma was so profound that Scottish essayist Thomas Carlyle described him as 'a magnificent specimen; you might say to all the world, this is our chief man.'

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 246: John C. Calhoun—Nullification, the Cast-Iron Man, and the Road to Secession. Until then, stay curious.
